query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A self-reinforcing degradation cycle arises from wear-induced removal of a protective oxide film that, once disrupted, intensifies local galvanic corrosion. The ensuing corrosive attack further weakens the film, creating a positive feedback loop that accelerates overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high–entropy alloy produced via laser melting deposition, exhibiting a dual-phase microstructure with a naturally forming oxide film during high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to combined sliding wear in a chloride-containing corrosive medium at an elevated temperature of 900 °C under steady sliding conditions.
generation.conditions: Constant high temperature (∼900 °C) with a corrosive medium containing chloride ions, and under a fixed load sliding contact that cyclically disrupts the surface oxide.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity of the cyclically damaged oxide film at phase boundaries that mediates both friction and corrosion processes.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the friction-induced spallation removes portions of the protective oxide film. This removal exposes heterogeneous metal surfaces with differing corrosion potentials, generating localized galvanic cells that accelerate corrosion. The accelerated corrosion further disrupts the oxide’s reformation, thereby driving a self-reinforcing cycle of wear and corrosion that culminates in rapid material degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significantly higher overall degradation rate (potentially a doubling of total material loss) relative to baselines where only wear or only corrosion is present. Individual measurements will indicate increased wear track depth and a greater number and size of corrosion pits.
generation.baseline: Control experiments where the alloy is subjected to only wear (in inert atmosphere) or only corrosion (static exposure) under identical temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: A critical sliding frequency and corrosive ion concentration must be reached to trigger the feedback cycle; below these thresholds, degradation rates will be lower.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative balance between oxide removal, reformation kinetics, and galvanic current density introduces uncertainty in predicting exact material loss rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples. One set is left untreated, while the other is pre-coated with a stabilized oxide film (e.g., through controlled pre-oxidation or surface treatment). Subject both sets to identical combined wear and corrosion testing at 900 °C in a chloride-laden environment. Compare degradation rates, oxide integrity over time, and local corrosion behavior.
measurements: Total material loss (mass loss or wear track volume)
SEM analysis of corrosion pit morphology and density
Time-resolved monitoring of oxide film thickness and spallation events
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples with a stabilized oxide film do not show a significantly reduced degradation rate (i.e., if the self-reinforcing cycle is not mitigated), or if degradation rates in the coupled tests are only additive of independent wear and corrosion effects rather than synergistic, the hypothesis is falsified.

This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance. Based on the above conclusions, the corrosion process of the EHEA in the test solution is schematically described in Figure 14. The passive films of few Al-Ni-rich phases are attacked by Cl− at lower temperature (Figure 14a2), and then occurs localized corrosion (Figure 14a3); while the passive films of Al-Ni-rich phases are damaged (Figure 14b2), and more Al-Ni-rich phases are dissolved at higher temperature (Figure 14b3). Metastable pits are preferentially created on the grain boundary or B2 phase. Pitting is enhanced by the effect of polarization. Due to autocatalysis by the caustic ions, the metastable pits gradually grow in the pitting corrosion area or the selective dissolution region. Moreover, the size of the selective dissolution region increases with temperature, and pitting occurs on the surface at various temperatures.

papers.title: Influence of Laser Power on CoCrFeNiMo High-Entropy Alloy Coating Microstructure and Properties.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy coating prepared by laser cladding
papers.approach: Variation of laser power (2000 W, 2250 W, 2500 W) to control eutectic/hypereutectic microstructure; SEM imaging and mechanical (wear) testing.
papers.findings: At 2250 W, a eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure forms with refined grain sizes and a mixed tri-phase structure (black/gray/white phases). The coating exhibited increased hardness and lower coefficient of friction due to formation of a protective oxide film that later undergoes stress accumulation and spallation.
papers.mechanism: A protective oxide layer forms during high-speed wear, initially reducing friction; however, under prolonged cyclic shear it accumulates stress and fractures, exposing brittle σ-phase or similar constituents. This spallation then accelerates both wear loss and corrosion attack via exposure of reactive surfaces.

papers.title: High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy produced by spark plasma sintering (SPS)
papers.approach: Reciprocating wear tests from room temperature up to 900 °C combined with XRD, SEM, and microhardness measurements to assess wear depth, oxide layer formation, and friction behaviors.
papers.findings: Wear resistance initially decreases with temperature up to 500 °C and then improves markedly at higher temperatures (800–900 °C) due to formation of a protective oxide film (including spinel phases). The COF decreases at higher test temperatures.
papers.mechanism: The formation of a protective oxide/spinel layer at elevated temperature plays a dual role; it provides a lubricating effect and acts as a diffusion barrier. However, the interface between the oxide and the underlying alloy is sensitive to mechanical disruption, which can trigger accelerated degradation if the barrier is compromised under combined wear and corrosive conditions.

papers.title: Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation.
papers.system: Ni-based complex concentrated alloy (NiX) with engineered nanohierarchical architecture
papers.approach: Design of alloys with nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates; wear testing at room temperature and elevated temperatures; nanoindentation and cross-sectional microstructural observation.
papers.findings: Demonstrated ultralow wear rates (10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm) over a wide temperature range. The alloy forms a dense glaze layer at high temperatures, while a counterpart (Ni3X) shows adhesive wear with oxide spallation and delamination.
papers.mechanism: The concept of adaptive friction interface protection is proposed where nanohierarchical architecture facilitates stress accommodation and multiple deformation pathways; however, mechanical instability in the oxide layer (if not well integrated with the underlying microstructure) leads to friction-induced spallation, thereby contributing to coupled wear–corrosion degradation.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperature
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) with dual-phase lamellar (FCC and BCC/B2) structure
papers.approach: Electrochemical testing, EBSD, SKPFM, and microstructural analyses in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at varying temperatures.
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits stable passive films at low temperatures but develops unstable passive films with pitting at higher temperatures. There is a clear phase-specific difference: the B2 phase (enriched with Al and Ni) tends to pit and dissolve, while the FCC (or L12) phase remains more protective.
papers.mechanism: Micro-galvanic coupling between dissimilar phases (due to different potentials and dislocation densities) leads to accelerated localized corrosion under elevated temperature. The interface between phases becomes a site for preferential film breakdown and pitting, which, when combined with wear removal of the protective layer, accelerates overall degradation.

papers.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coatings with varying B additions on Q235 steel substrates
papers.approach: Laser cladding with boron microalloying; SEM/EDS characterization; tribological and electrochemical testing to assess wear and corrosion resistance.
papers.findings: Boron addition refines the microstructure by preserving BCC and σ phases and inducing in situ TiB2 formation. Moderate B content (x = 1) leads to the highest wear resistance with predominantly abrasive and oxidative wear, while lower B content enhances passive film stability and corrosion resistance.
papers.mechanism: Microalloying with B promotes lattice distortion and formation of fine TiB2 particles, which enhance the stability of the protective oxide/passive films under combined wear and corrosion conditions. There is an interplay between microstructure refinement and oxide film integrity that determines the overall degradation response.

established: Protective oxide films form on HEA surfaces during sliding wear at elevated temperatures, reducing friction but being vulnerable to spallation.
Multiphasic (eutectic) microstructures in HEAs lead to galvanic coupling, where differences in phase chemistry and defects (e.g., dislocation density) promote localized corrosion.
Processing conditions (laser power, SPS, post-heat treatment) significantly influence the microstructure and, hence, both wear and corrosion responses.

approaches_tried.approach: Modulation of laser cladding parameters (laser power, hatch spacing) to control microstructure in CoCrFeNiMo and ferritic stainless steel systems.
approaches_tried.outcome: Optimized laser power produces a refined eutectic structure that initially improves wear resistance via protective oxide formation, but inadequate energy input results in heterogeneous microstructures prone to accelerated degradation.

approaches_tried.approach: Spark plasma sintering to produce fine multiphase HEA microstructures and testing under reciprocating wear conditions at high temperatures.
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved wear resistance at high temperatures due to formation of protective oxide/spinel phases, although mechanical spallation still occurs under severe conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Alloying additions (B, Mo, Ti) and post-heat treatment to refine phase distributions and enhance passive film stability.
approaches_tried.outcome: Optimized alloy compositions show enhanced combined wear and corrosion resistance by stabilizing oxide films, but over-addition of alloying elements can lead to defects that reduce performance.

mechanisms: Formation and mechanical instability (spallation) of protective oxide layers under cyclic sliding at elevated temperatures.
Micro-galvanic coupling between dissimilar phases (e.g., FCC/L12 vs B2 or σ phases) that promotes localized corrosion, especially when the protective film is disrupted.
Adaptive friction interface protection via nanohierarchical architecture that can buffer stress gradients but may fail if oxide films delaminate.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize the beneficial role of oxide formation (reducing friction and wear), while others highlight that oxide spallation and the subsequent exposure of brittle phases accelerates degradation.

Differences in phase stability: while certain microstructures (eutectic or nanohierarchical) are reported to enhance performance, the role of specific phases (FCC vs BCC/B2 vs σ) in governing corrosion remains debated.
open_questions: What is the dominant single mechanistic explanation that accounts for the synergy between wear-induced oxide film spallation and accelerated galvanic corrosion in multiphase eutectic HEAs?

How do specific microstructural features (e.g., eutectic spacing, phase distribution, nanoprecipitates) interact with the dynamic formation and removal of protective oxide layers under simultaneous wear and corrosion?
Under what controlled environmental and mechanical conditions can one decouple the contributions of wear and corrosion to total degradation?
opportunities: Designing controlled comparative experiments by subjecting a matched eutectic HEA baseline to isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and coupled wear–corrosion conditions at a specific elevated temperature (e.g., 900 °C) in atmospheres with chloride/salt species.
Investigating the impact of microalloying (e.g., Boron or Mo additions) and post-heat treatment on stabilizing oxide films and reducing micro-galvanic corrosion effects in multiphase HEAs.

Developing in situ diagnostics (e.g., high-temperature microscopy, potential mapping under sliding) to directly observe the formation and spallation of oxide films and correlate them with localized corrosion events.
Exploring the integration of adaptive friction interface protection architectures with controlled phase distribution to mitigate coupled degradation.

directions.direction: In situ mechanistic studies using high‐temperature wear–corrosion testing and real‐time microscopy to directly observe the formation, stress–induced spallation, and regrowth of the protective oxide film at multiphase boundaries.
directions.assessment: This approach directly captures the dynamic interplay between mechanical removal of the oxide and its role in mediating galvanic corrosion at phase interfaces. Known physics of oxide formation and spallation support this method, though high‐temperature in situ testing is challenging.

directions.direction: Modelling and simulation of the local stress fields and electrochemical potential gradients at phase boundaries in a eutectic HEA under cyclic loading, to quantify how wear‐induced oxide damage accelerates local corrosion.
directions.assessment: This computational approach directly attacks the mechanistic query by elucidating critical thresholds for oxide failure and galvanic current initiation. It is based on well‐established continuum and electrochemical models but requires careful validation against experiments.

directions.direction: Alloy microalloying and post‐heat treatment to modify the multiphase microstructure (e.g. by slight B or Mo addition) in order to stabilize the protective oxide and reduce galvanic differences between phases.
directions.assessment: By altering composition and phase distribution, this method tests the hypothesis that degraded oxide integrity drives the coupled degradation. The evidence supports that alloying can stabilize oxides; however, achieving controlled modifications without introducing new defects may be challenging.

directions.direction: Controlled comparative experiments that decouple wear from corrosion by testing identical eutectic HEA samples under isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and coupled wear–corrosion conditions at elevated temperature.
directions.assessment: This method can directly distinguish the synergistic effect by comparing total degradation rates and phase‐specific attack between test conditions. It respects all constraints, is underpinned by previous work and is highly informative though careful environmental control is necessary.

directions.direction: Surface potential mapping (e.g., SKPFM) along with localized stress mapping to correlate oxide spallation sites with micro-galvanic activity at interphase boundaries in eutectic HEAs.
directions.assessment: Mapping the local electrochemical potentials and stresses provides direct evidence for the hypothesised driving force behind accelerated degradation. This approach is technically demanding but can yield quantitative correlations consistent with established corrosion theories.
